Excellency, Mr. Khalilur Rahman, President of the United Nations General Assembly. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, at the outset, allow me to congratulate His Excellency, Mr. Khalilur Rahman on his election as President of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. We meet at a time when tensions are growing, conflicts are multiplying, trust is eroding, and uncertainty is becoming part of our daily reality. Over the past several days, from this very rostrum, we have heard many delegations speak about the importance of peace. peace remains our most fundamental responsibility. But peace cannot be taken for granted. It must be diligently built, and it must be steadfastly protected, and it must be passed on to future generations. It is precisely in this spirit that Tajikistan initiated the proclamation of 2027 2036 at the International Decade of Strengthening Peace for Future Generations, which was adopted by the General Assembly resolution on 25 June 2026. We are grateful to Member States, partners and the United Nations system for supporting this initiative of the President of the Republic of Tajikistan, His Excellency Mr. Emomali Rahmon. The idea behind the decade is simple. Our responsibility for peace does not end with our generation. We must work to resolve the conflicts of today, but we must also prevent the conflicts of tomorrow. Building on this vision, Tajikistan will convene a high-level international conference on peace in Dushanbe in June 2027, in cooperation with the United Nations Alliance of Civilizations, the United Nations Youth Office and other partners. The conference will help launch the decade and turn our shared commitment to peace into practical cooperation. Mr. President, our position on conflicts and disputes is clear. They must be resolved peacefully. through dialogue, diplomacy, negotiations, and in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations. In this context, the situation in Palestine remains a matter of deep concern to Tajikistan. The continuing suffering of civilians must end. We reiterate our call for a lasting ceasefire in Gaza and unhindered access to humanitarian assistance. Our position remains principled and consistent. A just and lasting peace can only be achieved through dialogue and diplomacy in accordance with international law and the relevant resolutions of the United Nations. Tajikistan reaffirms its support for the establishment of an independent and sovereign state of Palestine based on the 1967 borders and with East Jerusalem as its capital, living side by side with Israel in peace and security. But peace cannot endure in isolation. It needs development, opportunity, inclusion, and hope. Excellencies, lasting peace requires sustainable development. Yet, development remains deeply uneven. Climate change is accelerating. Inequality persists, and too many countries continue to face structural barriers to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. For developing countries, particularly mountainous and landlocked developing countries, these pressures are even greater. We therefore need stronger international solidarity and development financing that is more accessible, predictable and adequate. For Tajikistan, sustainable development begins at home. Our National Development Strategy 2030 remains a key framework for economic growth, reducing vulnerabilities, and improving the well-being of our people. But development is not only about economic growth. It is about people, opportunity, and inclusion. That is why Tajikistan continues to advance the empowerment of women and their meaningful participation in political, economic, and social life. It is also why we place growing emphasis on legal literacy. In 2025, the General Assembly proclaimed 2027 as the International Year of Legal Literacy, following an initiative of Tajikistan. Respect to the law strengthens peaceful and inclusive societies. But development also depends on something even more fundamental. something that connects people, economies, ecosystems, and nations, water. Mr. President, the world remains far from achieving universal access to safe water and sanitation. Progress is being made, but not fast enough. For Tajikistan, this challenges both global and deeply national. We are a mountainous country, home to thousands of glaciers and the source of major rivers that sustain communities far beyond our borders. We know the value of water, and we know its vulnerability. For more than two decades, under the leadership of President of Tajikistan, His Excellency Mr. Emomali Rahmon, water has remained at the heart of our international engagement. From the Global Water Action Decades to the Dushanbe Water Process, from the 2023 United Nations Water Conference to the Global Agenda on Glaciers Preservation. our message has remained consistent. Water requires cooperation, and cooperation must lead to action. The next two years will be decisive. Later this year, the international community will gather for the United Nations Water Conference in Abu Dhabi. In 2027, A high level preparatory meeting will take place here at United Nations headquarters. And in 2028, we will gather in Dushanbe for the United Nations Water Conference and the final comprehensive review of the Water Action Decade. Member states will negotiate and adopt by consensus an outcome, the Dushanbe Water Framework. This gives us an opportunity to assess what we have achieved, confront what remains unfinished, and decide how global water cooperation should move forward. Because 2028 must not be an end point. The conclusion of the Water Action Decade should mark the beginning of the next chapter of global water action. The Dushanbe Water Framework can help us write that chapter, a chapter focused on implementation, on financing, on technology and capacity, on stronger partnerships, and on protecting the sources of our water water, including the world's rapidly changing glaciers. Our objective is continuity, follow up and implementation. In this regard, the Dushanbe Water Process can help sustain that momentum beyond 2028, connecting global commitments with national and regional action. Our success will measured by the commitments we deliver. Excellencies, we must also prepare for a world that is changing before our eyes. Artificial intelligence is transforming our economies, our societies, and the way we approach development. As the Secretary-General recently reminded us, used well and shared widely, AI could compress decades of development into years. This is the opportunity before us. AI should not become another source of division. It should become a force for development, opportunity, and reducing inequality. Last year, at the initiative of Tajikistan, the General Assembly adopted the resolution on the role of artificial intelligence in creating new opportunities for sustainable development in Central Asia. This year, we look another step forward. On August 31st, the General Assembly proclaimed the International Day of Safe, Secure and Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence, also at the initiative of Tajikistan. Our message is simple. Innovation must serve humanity. Technological transformation is only one dimension of a rapidly changing world. Old threats are also evolving, and new ones are crossing borders faster than ever. Mr. President, terrorism and extremism, cybercrime, illicit trafficking in arms and narcotic drugs, organized crime -- these threats know no borders. Our response must be equally united. Therefore, the Dushanbe process on countering terrorism and its financing has become an important platform for international and regional cooperation. We will continue this engagement, including by convening the next high-level counterterrorism conference in Dushanbe in 2027. Mr. President, for our region, Lasting security and sustainable development are also closely linked to Afghanistan. Afghanistan needs peace, stability, and economic opportunity. Tajikistan will continue to support the Afghan people and constructive regional cooperation for a peaceful and stable Afghanistan. When Tajikistan speaks about peace, we also speak from experience. Next year, we will mark the 30th anniversary of the general agreement on the establishment of peace and national accord in Tajikistan. That agreement ended a devastating imposed civil war. It was achieved through dialogue, through compromise, and through the determination to put the future of the country above division. The United Nations was an important partner in that process. Three decades later, the same belief in dialogue continues to guide our relations with our neighbors. Recent agreements with Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan have helped resolved longstanding border issue and opened a new chapter of cooperation in Central Asia. Borders that once divided us can now connect us. Our experience has strengthened our convictions. Even the most difficult disagreements can be resolved when there is political will, dialogue, and mutual respect. Excellencies, There is a wider lesson here. Peace requires effective institutions, and international cooperation requires an effective United Nations. This is why Tajikistan supports the ongoing UN reform process. Reform is not an end in itself. It must make the United Nations more effective, agile, coherent and better able to deliver. We support reducing duplication, improving efficiency and strengthening accountability while preserving the organization's ability to fulfill its mandates. Member states must remain at the center of this process. Excellencies, a stronger UN also requires Member States willing to assume greater responsibility. Tajikistan is ready to do so. For the first time in its history, Tajikistan is seeking election to the United Nations Security Council for the 2028-2029 term. We approach this responsibility with humility and determination. We congratulate proudly Kyrgyzstan on its election to the Security Council for 2027-2028 and look forward to its contribution to the work of the Council. Tajikistan would bring the experience of a country that has known conflict and built peace, that has faced difficult borders and chosen dialogue and compromise, a country that shares a long border with Afghanistan and understands firsthand the importance of prevention, stability, and regional cooperation, and a country that has consistently advanced practical multilateral initiatives on water, glaciers, counter-terrorism, sustainable development and peace. For us, membership in the Security Council would not be about status. It would be about responsibility to uphold the Charter, to listen to all voices, large and small, to seek common ground where divisions persist, and to contribute constructively to the maintenance of international peace and security. Mr. President, we began with peace. Let me end with peace. The challenges before us are great, but they are not greater than our capacity to overcome them if we choose cooperation over confrontation, dialogue over division, and hope over fear. The choices we make today will shape the world we leave behind tomorrow. That is our responsibility to our peoples, to one another, and above all, to future generations. Tajikistan stands ready to do its part. I thank you for your attention.

I I thank the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Tajikistan for his presentation. I now give the floor to His Excellency Mohamed Ali Nafti, Minister for Foreign Affairs, Migration and Tunisians Abroad of Tunisia.

In the name of God, most merciful, most compassionate. May the peace of God be upon you. Mr. President, your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. At the outset, I would like to extend my sincere congratulations to his excellency, Mr. Khalilur Rahman, on his election as president of the 81st session of the General Assembly. I wish him every success in leading the work of this session. I would also like to express our deep appreciation and gratitude to the Secretary-General, Mr. Antonio Guterres, at the end of his term of office. for his wise leadership in the service of peace, security, development, and justice, and for his tireless efforts to preserve the standing of the Organization and restore confidence in multilateral action at a time of extraordinary international complexity, when maintaining the effectiveness of the United Nations has become a demanding responsibility. and an almost daily challenge. Mr. Guterres faced with courage and dedication unprecedented global crises. He leaves behind a significant legacy of committed diplomacy and principled positions that we shall continue to remember. At this critical historical juncture, for the United Nations, we look forward with great hope to the selection, through the process of electing the new Secretary-General, of the most capable and deserving individual to lead the Organization with a bold strategic vision, building upon the efforts of his predecessor and capable of providing practical solutions for the various regions whose peoples continue to suffer the consequences of crises, wars, instability and inequality. A vision that restores hope to future generations for a better future in which the conditions for a dignified life are available to all. Mr. President, we meet during this 81st session under the theme, "Restoring Trust and Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All." This prompts us to ask, how can we restore this trust? And before managing the desired transformation, how can we create the conditions and lay the foundations necessary for it? Our questions stem neither from doubt nor from pessimism, but from a firm conviction that restoring trust requires serious and responsible reflection on the reasons behind its decline. Tunisia's belief in multilateral action is not a product of current circumstances. Rather, it is the continuation of a journey that began before independence, when the national movement brought the cause of the Tunisian people before the United Nations and made the right to self-determination and the recovery of sovereignty an integral part of the struggle for freedom. Following independence, Tunisia engaged fully within the United Nations to complete the foundations of its sovereignty and to build the modern state, and it succeeded in doing so. Restoring confidence in the organization and in multilateral action requires, in our view, two essential conditions. A genuine commitment and a meaningful reform process. First, there must be a sincere determination and responsible commitment by all states to respect international law founded on agreements and the principle of sovereign equality among states, and to uphold the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, particularly refraining from the use of force, the settlement of disputes by peaceful means, and fulfilling international obligations in good faith. Second, the United Nations must embark on a comprehensive and profound reform process that responds to the transformations that have taken place in the world. This requires, in particular, reconsidering the mechanisms of decision making within the organization to ensure a more balanced and equitable geographical representation and establishing more effective mechanisms for transparency and accountability, thus reinforcing the confidence of states and peoples and the organization's ability to respond to the aspirations of all. Unless genuine progress is achieved on these two tracks, collective action will remain hostage to narrow geopolitical calculations. And the gap will continue to widen between the principles we agree upon and the realities we witness on the ground. We may choose either to continue meeting under the idealism of slogans or to commit ourselves to what can truly achieve development, prosperity, and peace for all. If we have the will, we have the capacity. Tunisia welcomes the efforts undertaken within the framework of the UN80 initiative. We regard these efforts as a true opportunity on which we should build. rather than a final destination in the reform process. We support the three reform tracks proposed by the initiative, provided that they are pursued through an inclusive consultative process that preserves the intergovernmental nature of the organization and does not undermine the negotiating mandates of member states. Tunisia also believes that addressing the liquidity crisis in the organization requires all states to meet their financial obligations in full. We stress that reform should not result in a reduction of support allocated to developing countries or to humanitarian missions and development programs supervised by the Organization and its specialized agencies. Tunisia, therefore, calls for a fair and balanced approach that safeguards both the effectiveness and credibility of the United Nations. Mr. President, Trust in the international system is measured by the extent to which its members adhere to the principles of the Charter and its resolutions, and by the organization's ability to ensure respect for international law without selectivity or double standards, and to protect the oppressed peoples who have no refuge except international legitimacy. How can we restore this trust while the Palestinian people are subjected daily to the most horrific crimes and violations and denied their most basic rights to life, security, freedom, and self-determination, while the international community remains unable to put an end to their ongoing humanitarian suffering or to enforce respect for international law and international humanitarian law? My country, Tunisia, condemns the continuing settlement policies of the occupying entity in the West Bank and the policies of persecution, starvation, and isolation in the Gaza Strip, and the crimes of genocide that claim more lives each day, in the absence of any accountability or any punishment. Tunisia calls upon the international community to shoulder its legal, moral and humanitarian responsibilities and to end this long-standing historical injustice. Tunisia recalls that the International Court of Justice in its advisory opinion of the 19th of July 2024 affirmed that the occupying entity is compelled to end its unlawful presence in the occupied Palestinian territory and that all UN member states are likewise compelled not to recognize as lawful the situation resulting from that unlawful presence. and that the United Nations, through its principal organs, should consider the means and measures required to bring that presence to an end as rapidly as possible. We further recall that the International Court of Justice, in the same advisory opinion, determined that the policies pursued by the occupying entity in Jerusalem form part of the process of annexation. and affirmed that the domestic law of the occupying power does not alter Jerusalem's international legal status. In this context, Tunisia reiterates its categorical rejection of all unilateral measures aimed at altering the historical, legal, and demographic character of Holy Jerusalem, including forced displacement, house demolitions, and repeated attacks on Islamic and Christian holy sites. The catastrophic humanitarian conditions endured by the Palestinian people, particularly in the Gaza Strip, as a result of continued casualties, displacement, the destruction of homes and infrastructure, and the collapse of the health care system, require safe, urgent, and sustained humanitarian access. It also requires allowing the UN and its specialized agencies to carry out their missions, especially the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East, UNRWA. Tunisia considers that any attempt to dismantle this long-standing UN agency or to undermine its mandate prior to a just and lasting solution to the Palestinian refugee issue

constitutes a desperate attempt to eliminate the right of return and to liquidate the Palestinian cause as a whole. The logic of force may be able to impose a bitter and inhumane reality for a period of time, but it can never break the will of peoples, nor halt the course of history. The will of peoples always finds its way and ultimately prevails. Such is the law of the universe and the course of history. Tunisia will remain steadfast in its support for the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people, which are not subject to prescription, foremost among them their right to establish an independent and fully sovereign state on the entirety of Palestine, with Al-Quds al-Sharif as its capital. Mr. President, Tunisia follows with deep concern the continuing escalation in the Middle East and its dangerous repercussions at the security, political and economic levels. Tunisia believes that the continuation of this situation will further complicate matters and could lead to catastrophic consequences for all countries of the region and the world. Tunisia renews its call for an immediate cessation of military operations. for wisdom and reason to prevail, and for a return to dialogue and negotiations, giving absolute priority to political and peaceful and diplomatic solutions as the only means of resolving existing disputes in a manner that strengthens the foundations of security and stability in the region and prevents further escalation. Tunisia also reaffirms its commitment to freedom of navigation and maritime security in accordance with the principles and provisions of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea and customary international law, while preserving global energy security, international supply chains, and the economic rights of states. Mr. President, given the bonds of brotherhood and good neighborliness that unite the Tunisian and Libyan peoples, as well as their shared interests and common destiny, Tunisia supports every sincere Libyan effort and every serious UN initiative aimed at ending the crisis on the basis of a Libyan-led and Libyan-owned solution founded on dialogue and consensus among all parties, preserving Libya's unity, sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the aspirations of the brotherly Libyan people for security, stability, and a unified state. Tunisia reiterates its full solidarity with the Lebanese Republic and stands by the Lebanese people. We are committed to Lebanon's sovereignty and independence, and we condemn the repeated violations of the ceasefire agreement in this brotherly country and a flagrant violation of UN resolutions. Tunisia calls for the United Nations to be enabled to fully discharge its mandate in the brotherly country of Lebanon. Tunisia also condemns the repeated Zionist attacks targeting the Syrian territory and the resources of the brotherly Syrian people. We express our hope that the Syrian people will succeed in preserving the unity, independence, and sovereignty of Syria over all its territory. Likewise, Tunisia follows with grave concern the continuing war in Sudan, and we renew our solidarity with the Sudanese people. Tunisia calls upon the United Nations to support all efforts aimed at achieving an immediate and permanent cessation of hostilities in the hope that Sudan may restore stability and security, turn the page on conflict, and focus on reconstruction and recovery. Tunisia also hopes that the Yemeni brothers will reach a comprehensive and lasting political settlement that restores security and stability to the Yemeni people and preserve the country's territorial integrity. Tunisia renews its support for regional and international efforts to find a solution to the crisis in Yemen. Mr. President, the abundant human resources, natural wealth, and the promising potential of Africa make Africa an essential partner in advancing development at the international level. Yet, the Africa we want continues to face intertwined security and economic challenges that require a comprehensive approach. In this regard, Tunisia reaffirms its commitment to the principle of African solutions to African problems, thereby strengthening the ownership of African countries and peoples over the resolution of their crises and reinforcing the role of African mechanisms and institutions in maintaining peace and security. Tunisia renews its support for the reform of the African Union so that it may better fulfill its responsibilities and respond effectively to current challenges. Tunisia also stresses the importance of strengthening the partnership between the United Nations and the African Union in conflict prevention, mediation, peacekeeping, peacebuilding, and sustainable development. In this context, Tunisia emphasizes its determination to continue contributing to peacekeeping efforts in Africa, a commitment it has maintained since the first years of its independence. Tunisia also reiterates its commitment to strengthen economic integration across the continent, particularly within the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa, COMESA, and the African Continental Free Trade Area. Mr. President, Tunisia believes that peace, security, and comprehensive development are inseparable. The essence of this session, a United Nations that delivers for all, lies in the organization's ability to serve all states and peoples according to their needs and commensurate to the challenges they face. Equality does not mean identical responses. Rather, it means ensuring that everyone benefits from the UN system while directing greater support and attention to those in greatest need and to the peoples and countries facing war, poverty, marginalization, and the effects of global crisis. The United Nations we seek is one that leaves no one behind, does not define need according to selective political criteria, and places justice, equity, and solidarity at the core of its services to all. Guided by its firm belief in the importance of investing in people, Tunisia once again calls for a comprehensive and balanced approach to migration that takes into account its human and historical dimensions and moves beyond a narrow security perspective while addressing its root causes, foremost among them conflict, poverty, economic and social disparities. lack of employment opportunities and development, and the proliferation of human trafficking networks. Such an approach would embody shared responsibility, solidarity, and cooperation among countries of origin, transit, and destination. In this context, the Tunisian authorities continue their efforts to save the lives of irregular migrants on land and at sea, provide them with care and create suitable conditions for their voluntary return to their countries of origin in coordination with the International Organization for Migration, while safeguarding their dignity and rights and combating human trafficking and migrant smuggling, and also supporting them once they are back in their countries of origin. Tunisia once again firmly rejects becoming either a transit country or a destination for irregular migrants who are victims of human trafficking networks. Believing that climate change is a major factor affecting development, security, and stability, Tunisia emphasizes that addressing this challenge requires a genuine climate justice particularly since developing countries bear severe consequences despite their limited historical responsibility for emissions. Accordingly, countries with the greatest responsibility must fulfill their commitments regarding climate finance while maintaining a clear distinction between climate financing and development financing. Tunisia believes that achieving climate justice Comprehensive development and pandemic preparedness and response requires reform of the international financial architecture to make it more equitable, inclusive, and fair, thus ensuring developing countries have easier and fairer access to financing and enabling them to invest in scientific research, technology, innovation, and digital transformation, thereby reducing their debt burdens, strengthening their resilience, and empowering them to rely on their own capacities in shaping their future. My country stresses that the rapid development of artificial intelligence offers great opportunities to accelerate development goals. provided that it is accompanied by comprehensive and equitable global governance that ensure that responsible use and prevents the widening of the digital divide between North and South through capacity building, technology transfer, and adequate financing. Mr. President, under the leadership of President Kais Saied, Tunisia reaffirms its unwavering determination to continue its reform process, launched on the 25th of July 2021, with the aim of consolidating a democracy that guarantees rights and freedoms for all citizens and responds to the aspirations of the Tunisian people for development and prosperity. My country relies primarily on its own resources and human potential. and remains committed to attracting investment, strengthening and diversifying economic partnerships based on mutual benefit, equality, and mutual respect in a manner that serves its interests and preserves the independence of its decision making. In this context, Tunisia reaffirms its steadfast commitment to human rights and public and individual freedoms in accordance with the constitution of the 25th of July, 2022, its international obligations and the choices of its people. We stress the importance of promoting the comprehensive and interconnected nature of human rights, including economic, climate-related, social, scientific, cultural, and educational rights, foremost among them, the fundamental right to development. We believe that the success of reform and development depends on the participation of women and youth. Therefore, Tunisia emphasizes its commitment to strengthening the role of women in public life and in decision-making positions, and to continuing efforts to combat all forms of violence and discrimination against women, recognizing that women's empowerment is a key driver of development and stability. Likewise, Tunisia places youth at the heart of its national priorities and works to empower them politically, economically, and socially, while encouraging their initiatives and their participation in public affairs and decision-making. I also take this opportunity to commend all members of the Tunisian diaspora, wherever they may be, in recognition of their role in enhancing Tunisia's image abroad and supporting development efforts in their homeland. We reaffirm the President's continuous commitment to strengthening support programs for the diaspora and further consolidating ties with them so that our diaspora may continue to serve as a living example of successful integration in their countries of residence. Mr. President, Tunisia firmly believes that peace operations cannot be limited to crisis management and conflict containment. Rather, they must contribute to creating conditions conducive to sustainable peace through supporting state institutions, the rule of law, the empowerment of local communities, and enhancing development. Tunisia reaffirms its readiness to continue contributing to the development of the peacekeeping system in ways that enhance its effectiveness and credibility. Drawing on our long-standing and active participation in UN peacekeeping operations, Tunisia believes that advancing these operations requires investment in human and institutional capacities and a greater protection of civilians as a collective responsibility and humanitarian imperative. In this regard, Tunisia calls for building upon the outcomes of the international conference hosted by Tunisia in July 2025 in cooperation with the UN Department of Peace Operations on the role of armed forces and the protection of civilians. including through the establishment of an international platform for exchanging expertise and information, the development of a unified operational manual, and the strengthening of training, capacity building, and civil-military coordination, which should include both men and women. Mr. President, in conclusion, I wish to reaffirm that the United Nations remains for Tunisia, the home of international legitimacy, the house that carries the hopes and aspirations of future generations for a more just and equitable international order, and a unique forum for finding practical solutions to achieve the balance of peace, security, and comprehensive and sustainable development in accordance with the UN 2030 agenda. I thank you for your kind attention. May the peace and mercy of God be upon you.

The 14th plenary meeting of the General Assembly is called to order. The Assembly will continue its consideration of agenda item 8, entitled General Debate. I now give the floor to His Excellency Lukura Bakari, Minister of Foreign Affairs, Political Affairs, International Economic Cooperation and Digital Transition of San Marino.

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary General, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, San Marino is the world's oldest republic. For more than 17 centuries, we have survived not through military power, territorial expansion, economic might, but through dialogue, respect for the law, neutrality, and the conviction that sovereignty of a small state is no less valuable than that of a great power. Our history has taught a simple lesson. When power is not enough to protect you, rule matter. When you cannot impose your will, dialogue matter. And when the world is divided, institutions that bring states together matter. This is why multilateralism is not an abstract concept for San Marino. It's a fundamental principle of our foreign policy and, in many ways, a lesson drawn from our own history. Our commitment to cooperation and shared rule is also reflected in our relationship with the European Union. The forthcoming signing of the association agreement with the European Union on 19 October will mark a milestone for our country. It represents an historical step toward closer cooperation, shared rule, and greater integration within the European Union, while fully preserving our sovereignty, identity, and institutional specificity. For San Marino, this is not simply an agreement about economic relation. It's a long-term choice to deepen our engagement with Europe while preserving the distinctive character of our republic. It is a choice that reflect a principle at the heart of our history. Cooperation does not diminish sovereignty. For a small state, cooperation, rule, and dialogue are precisely what allow sovereignty to be exercised and protected. Today, that principle is under extraordinary pressure. 81 years ago, the United Nations was created to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war. Yet today, conflicts are multiplying, inequalities are deepening, climate disruption is accelerating, food and water are increasingly being used as an instrument of pressure, and the rules that have governed international relations for decades are being challenged. We are witnessing the use of force against a sovereign state. We are witnessing violation of international law, humanitarian and human rights law. At such a moment, the answer cannot be less multilateralism. It must be more. And it must be a multilateral that works, that protects the weak as well the strong, on that apply the law equality, and one that give every state, large or small, a meaningful voice. Before turning to the challenge before us, allow me to congratulate His Excellency, Dr. Kalyu Raman, on his election as a president of the 81st section of the General Assembly. San Marino support the priority of your program and stand ready to cooperate fully with you and with all member states in the year ahead. I also wish to express our appreciation to Secretary General Antonio Guterres for his leadership at a time of profound international unsustainability and for his continuing effort to strain the United Nations multilateral system. Mr. President, there can be no world in which might make right. Sovereignty, territorial integrity, political independence, and self-determination matter. These principles are not optional, and they cannot depend on the size of a country or the power of a government. There can be no impunity for violation of international law. The law must apply to all. For San Marino, this is not an abstract principle. For small state, international law is our protection. It is the ultimate equalizer. A rule-based international order allow every state, large or small, to have an equal voice and equal legal standing. This is why San Marino strongly support the Secretary General UN initiative. The United Nation must become more effective more efficient and more responsive. And reform must include the Security Council. The Council must better reflect today's world. It must be more representative, transparent and accountable. San Marino is also a member of the Uniting for Consensus group and supports its effort to promote a comprehensive and balanced reform of the Security Council. based on a greater regional representation, equitable geographical distribution, and wider access to elected seat. Reform must train the voice of all member states, including the small state, and it must be achieved through broad consensus. We support effort to restrain the use of the veto, including the French-Mexican initiative and the ACT code of conduct in a situation involving mass atrocity alongside the General Assembly veto initiative. We also reaffirm our full support for the International Court of Justice. Its order and judgment are legally binding. Mr. President, the next Secretary-General will carry a vital responsibility. The United Nations must remain relevant and credible. Above all, it must remain capable of protecting people and upholding the Charter. San Marino stands ready to contribute. I now turn to one of the most painful crises of our time. The situation in the Middle East demands clarity. San Marino unequivocally condemns terrorism, including the horrific attack of 7 October 2023. But we must be equally clear on another point. The Palestinian people have an annihilable right to self-determination and to their own state. Statehood is not a reward for terrorism. It's a right. At the same time, nothing can justify the collective punishment of civilians. The suffering in Gaza cannot become new normal. We call for a permanent ceasefire and for full, safe, and and the read humanitarian access. Humanitarian assistance must reach those who need it. Civilian live must be protected. UNRWA and other humanitarian organizations must be able to operate. We call for the permanent disarmament of Hamas and other non-state armed group and for the withdrawal of Israeli force from the Gaza Strip. We support the Palestinian Authority and its reform efforts, including democratic election. We urge Israel to release withheld clearance revenue and to facilitate correspondent banking service for the Palestinian Authority. In the West Bank and the East Jerusalem settlement expansion, settled violence, land appropriation, demolition and eviction must stop. The situation is rapidly deteriorating. I mean, the presidential level of settled violence and settlement expansion included in an unacceptable decision to punish tender for the E1 settlement project. This development undermined the possibility of a viable Palestinian state. The status quo of Jerusalem holy site must be respected. All community, including Christian community, must be protected. Last year, San Marino endorsed the New York Declaration for a two-state solution. Following an unanimous mandate from our Parliament, the Great and General Council of San Marino recognized Palestine as a sovereign and independent state within secure and internationally recognized borders and in accordance with relevant United Nations resolutions. We stand by that decision. There is no alternative to the two-state living side by side in peace, security, and mutual recognition. The window for that solution is narrowing. We must act now. Mr. President, the consequences of the conflict extended far beyond Gaza and the West Bank. Escalation across the region, threatening international peace and security. We are deeply concerned by hostility involving Iran and by threat to maritime security in the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz. Freedom of navigation is essential to global stability. International law, including the UN close, must be respected in Lebanon. We call for full respect for sovereignty and for the implementation of Security Council Resolution 1701. Civilian infrastructure must be protected. In Syria, we support an inclusive and peaceful political transition that respects sovereignty, protects civilians, and strengthens institutions. Peace cannot be imposed by force. It requires diplomacy and dialogue. And it requires international role. Mr. President, Europe is also facing a war that continues to cause immense humanitarian suffering. San Marino condemns Russia's ongoing aggression against Ukraine, the bombardment of cities, the killing of civilians, attacks on humanitarian workers, the unlawful deportation of children. These are not simply tragedies; they are violations of international law. No state can be allowed to redraw borders by force. San Marino, therefore, reiterates its call for a full, immediate and unconditional cease-fire, leading to a comprehensive, just and lasting peace. Any peace must respect Ukrainian sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders. Mr. President. From Ukraine to Gaza, from Sudan to Syria, from the Sahel to Afghanistan, civilians continue to pay the highest price. Women, children, older people, families forced from their homes, hospitals and schools destroyed, food, water and medicine denied. International humanitarian law was created precisely for these circumstances. It does not disappear in time of war. It is not suspended by political convenience. It must be respected. San Marino strongly condemns the use of explosive weapons in populated areas and calls for all states to implement the Political Declaration on Explosive Weapons in Populated Areas. Those who deliver humanitarian assistance must also be protected. aid workers and journalists are not legitimate targets. San Marino also reaffirmed its commitment to the Australia-led declaration for the protection of humanitarian personnel and called on all parties to armed conflict to respect and protect humanitarian personnel and to ensure that assistance can reach those in need. Impunity cannot become normal. San Marino, therefore, reaffirms its commitment to the Geneva Convention, the Genocide Convention, and the Roman Statute. And we reiterate our unwavering support for the International Criminal Court. The court exists because the gravest crime cannot go unanswerable. Genocide, war crime, and crime against humanity. Accountability is not an obstacle to peace. It is a part of a lasting peace. The fight against impunity is also an essential element of the responsibility to protect, which must remain a shared responsibility of the international community. Recent political pressure and coercive measures against the Court, its officials and those who cooperate with it are deeply concerning. state parties to the Rome Statute must defend the independence and integrity of the Kurds. San Marino also reaffirmed its historic commitment to the abolition of the death penalty, which it abolished in 1865. This reflects our enduring conviction that human dignity must be protected even in the face of the gravest crime. Justice cannot depend on political power. Mr. President, five years ago, the Taliban seized power in Afghanistan. Five years is too long for half of our population to be denied its right. Afghan women and girls continue to face a systematic restriction on education, employment, movement, public participation, and access to justice. Girls remain excluded from secondary and higher education, women are increasingly excluded from public life. This cannot become normal. San Marino called for the full restoration of the right of Afghan women and girls. Education is a right, work is a right, participation in public life is a right, dignity is a right. These rights do not disappear because a government choose to deny them. The international community must continue to stand with Afghan women and girls. Humanitarian access must also remain underrated. Afghanistan must not be forgotten. Mr. President, children everywhere deserve protection. Children are being killed, maimed, abducted, and recruited. They are losing their home, their school, and their future. San Marino remain firmly committed to the children and harm the conflict agenda and support the work of the UN Special Representative for children in harm and conflict. School must remain safe place. We have endorsed the safe school declaration, the Paris principle and the Vancouver principle. We call on all state to strain the protection of children in armed conflict and the ratify the optional protocol of the convention of the right of the child. Mr. President, the return of nuclear threat is another source of grave concern. There can be no acceptable nuclear threat or acceptable use of nuclear weapon. The modernization and expansion of nuclear arsenal, together with growing military expenditure and the rapid development of artificial intelligences and cyber capabilities, increase the risk of escalation. The consequences of nuclear use will be catastrophic. San Marino remain committed to a world free of nuclear weapons. We support the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. We also proudly uphold the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, which San Marino has signed and ratified. Diplomacy must prevail over deterrence through fear. Peace and security cannot be separated from development. Nor can development be separated from human right. Conflict destroyed development gain. Poverty, food, instability. Climate change increased pressure on food, water, and community. We must also not overlook the devastating humanitarian and social and economic situation in Cuba. where prolonged hardship is placing an immense burden on the daily life of the Cuban people. We must therefore treat peace, security, human rights, and sustainable development as part of the same agenda. The SDG remain our common commitment. The Pact for the Future provide an opportunity to strain multilateralism and accelerate implementation of the 2030 agenda. But commitments are not enough. We need implementation, financing, and accountability. We also need a fair and more inclusive international financial architecture supported by adequate resources and greater financial stability for the UN itself. The triple planetary crisis, climate change, biodiversity, loss and pollution is already affecting peace and security. Environmental degradation, food insecurity, water scarcity and displacement. The Paris Agreement must be fully implemented. The 1.5 degree goal must remain within reach. The transition must be just and no country should be left behind. Food security must also remain at the heart of our collective effort. Conflict and climate shock are driving hunger and malnutrition. San Marino believes that reducing food loss and waste is one practical contribution of a more secure and sustainable food system. We are also entering a new technological era. Artificial intelligence and emerging technology offer enormous opportunity, but they also create new risks. Technology must serve humanity. It must not be used to undermine human rights. international peace or international humanitarian law. The rule must keep peace with innovation. And where new technology creates new risks, our responsibility is not to look away, but to govern them. This is why multilateralism matters. Multilateralism is not an out-of-date idea. It is not only a framework capable of managing an independent world. No country can address today's challenge alone, protect itself from climate change alone, prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons alone, or regulate global technology alone. And no country can build a lasting peace alone. We need cooperation and institutions that work. And we need the political courage to uphold the rule we have created together. Mr. President, for more than 17 centuries, San Marino has showed that a small state can preserve its independence through dialogue, respect for the law, and engagement with the international community. This is why San Marino will continue to defend the United Nations Charter, international law, human rights, and multilateralism. At a time when the world is tempted by division, we must choose cooperation. When force challenge law, we must stand firmly by the law. And when the spirits grow, we must choose peace. San Marino will do its part. Together, we must ensure that the United Nations remain what it was created to be, a shield for the vulnerable, a forum of dialogue, and a guardian of peace, dignity, and international law. Thank you.

I thank the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Political Affairs, International Economic Cooperation and Digital Transition of San Marino. I now give the floor to His Excellency Abdelkader Hussein Omar, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Government Spokesperson of Djibouti.

At the outset, I should like to convey to this august assembly the greetings of His Excellency Ismael Omar Guelleh, President of the Republic of Djibouti. Mr. President, allow me, on behalf of the Republic of Djibouti, to extend my warm congratulations to His Excellency Mr. Khalilur Rahman of Bangladesh on his election as President of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, and to wish him every success in carrying out his mandate. I would also like to pay tribute to Her Excellency Madam Annalena Baerbock for her leadership during the last session, which marked the 80th anniversary of our organization. The Republic of Djibouti welcomes the choice of the theme for this session, Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation, a United Nations that Delivers for All. This theme is particularly relevant in the current international context. We're living through a critical juncture exacerbated by the proliferation of conflicts, deepening existing crises and the emergence of conflicts and the emergence of new crises with devastating political, economic, humanitarian and security consequences. In the face of these challenges, we must reaffirm the essential mission of the United Nations and strengthen a renewed, more inclusive and more effective multilateralism that takes full account of the interests of all States, large and small. The region that is home to my country also continues to face crises, the consequences of which extend beyond our national borders. Djibouti is following the situation in Yemen with grave concern. We are indeed directly experiencing its effects with the recent arrival in our territory of several thousand people fleeing the violence. This situation is already placing considerable pressure on host communities in the Obock region, as well as on the reception capacity of the Markazai site. Djibouti alone cannot meet the growing needs for shelter, food and essential services. Therefore, we reiterate our appeal to the international community to step up its support so that we can respond adequately to this influx, which, according to UN estimates, could reach up to 10,000 people. In order to prevent this humanitarian crisis from becoming protracted, we renew our call for de-escalation and for a lasting political solution in Yemen to preserve human life. Turning now to Somalia, we remain fully committed to the Somali people and government in their quest to consolidate peace and stability. The international community must preserve the security gains that have been made and continue to support the Somali authorities in fully shouldering their responsibilities and protecting their institutions. In this regard, we recognize the crucial role played by AUSOM in stabilizing the country, as well as the crucial support provided by the United Nations, particularly through UNSOS. We hope that the international community will stand mobilized so as to enable Somalis to assume lasting responsibility for their security, sovereignty, and the preservation of the integrity of their national territory. Turning now to Sudan, Djibouti, in its capacity as current chair of IGAD, welcomes the return of that kindred country to full participation in our regional organization, which is a founding member. We call for de-escalation and the resumption of talks to be prioritized. Only an inclusive political solution that places the Sudanese people at the heart of every initiative will make it possible to restore lasting peace and stability. We also call on foreign actors to refrain from fueling this war through harmful interference. Once again, we extend a hand to our Eritrean neighbor. Djibouti remains convinced that dialogue and negotiation in full respect for international law represent the only path towards a peaceful and definitive settlement of our border dispute and the return of our prisoners of war, who have been held incommunicado for more than 18 years. The Republic of Djibouti further reaffirms its unwavering solidarity with the Palestinian people and its full support for their legitimate rights, in particular their inalienable right to the establishment of an independent and sovereign State. We reaffirm our commitment to a two-State solution based on the 1967 borders. with East Jerusalem as the capital of the State of Palestine, as the path towards a just and lasting peace. We roundly condemn illegal settlement activity, violence committed against civilians, including by Israeli settlers in the West Bank, forced displacement, and any policy aimed at altering the demographic and territorial reality of the occupied Palestinian territory. The humanitarian situation in Gaza remains a tragedy requiring an immediate response from the international community. The protection of civilians must be guaranteed, humanitarian assistance must reach those in need without hindrance, and violations of international humanitarian law must cease and be condemned. Djibouti will continue to support efforts to bring an end to the suffering of the Palestinian people and to ensure that justice, peace and international law prevail. Preserving freedom of navigation in the Red Sea, and more particularly through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, is a major geopolitical and economic issue for regional and global stability. This strategic maritime passage is a vital artery for international trade, and any obstruction to free movement of shipping could seriously affect supply chains and energy security. Although Djibouti has observed no disruption to passage through the strait to date, my country's authorities remain particularly watchful with regard to the current tensions affecting the region. Mr. President, the climate emergency is one of the most pressing challenges facing our international community. For Djibouti, as an African coastal country, this emergency is indivisible from development. Rising sea levels pose a direct and growing threat to our populations and ecosystems. Djibouti, like many developing countries, makes only a marginal contribution to global emissions, yet remains particularly exposed to the consequences of climate disruption. This situation highlights a profound injustice. Those countries that have contributed least to climate change are often those that suffer its most severe consequences. We must therefore accelerate the implementation of the Paris Agreement and strengthen our adaptation and resilience efforts, including through resilient coastal infrastructure, better protection for marine and coastal ecosystems, early warning systems, and simplified, predictable, and equitable access to climate finance. For Djibouti, climate action must not be separated from development. On the contrary, it must help to transform our economies. develop renewable energy, create jobs, and open up new opportunities for investment and innovation. And it's in this spirit that the government is working to operationalize the mechanisms provided for under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement through a robust, transparent, and credible national framework for carbon markets, with a view to mobilizing new resources, attracting investment, promoting technology transfer and strengthening national capacities. This transformation, however, requires resources. Developing countries continue to face high financing costs, external vulnerabilities and limited fiscal space. Access to climate finance and reform of the international financial architecture therefore remain essential. In this regard, the CBI commitment represents an important step forward whose commitments must now be translated into tangible results, including through improved access to concessional financing, enhanced debt sustainability, and increased mobilization of public and private capital for development. We must also strengthen South-South and triangular cooperation in order to share technologies, knowledge, and solutions tailored to the realities of our countries. Africa must not be viewed solely as a region vulnerable to climate change. It should be recognized as an actor that is capable of innovating, proposing solutions, and contributing to the transformation of the global economy. Beyond climate action, the 2030 agenda remains at the heart of our development vision. Djibouti's economy is demonstrating resilience, driven in particular by port and logistics activities. trade, telecommunications, energy and investment. Djibouti intends to consolidate its role as a regional hub while accelerating the diversification of our economy. This ambition can be seen just as recently as this week with the launch of construction work on modern petroleum product storage facilities and transport infrastructure, including oil and gas pipelines in Djibouti, linking Djibouti and Ethiopia. These projects illustrate our ambition to achieve energy sovereignty and security, regional integration and economic transformation. But above all, growth should translate into jobs, social progress and opportunities, particularly for women and young people. We are continuing to invest in education, health, and to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals and implement the African Union's Agenda 2063. Both require a collective surge of action. The climate emergency demands action, development demands investment, and peace and humanitarian crises demand solidarity. The digital transition and artificial intelligence also offer new opportunities to accelerate development and improve the capacities of our states. Their potential, however, will only be fully realized if we are able to bridge the digital divide, facilitate technology sharing, and build the capacities of developing countries. And with that in mind, Djibouti supports the beyond GDP intergovernmental process. This seeks to complement traditional economic indicators with measures that better take into account people's well-being, social inclusion and environmental sustainability. and problem solvers. We learned very early that influence does not depend only on size or power. Mr. President, for Jamaica, the consequences of global challenges are not theoretical. On the 28th of October last year, Hurricane Melissa struck our island. In a matter of hours, the most catastrophic hurricane in our modern history inflicted damage and loss estimated at 56.7% of our GDP. Think about that. In a matter of hours, more than half the value of an entire year of national economic output was damaged or lost. A single event. Jamaica had prepared. Years of fiscal discipline had allowed us to build buffers. We had put in place disaster risk financing, including catastrophe insurance, and an independently sponsored catastrophe bond. Those measures gave us immediate liquidity. But no level of prudent national planning can fully insulate a small developing state from a climate event of that magnitude. And therein lies the fundamental inequity faced by small island developing states. We can do everything right. Jamaica has not simply resolved to recover. We have resolved to rebuild better and differently. Our resilience must not be measured by how much suffering we can withstand. It must be measured by how well we prepare, how quickly we recover, how intelligently we adapt, and whether we emerge stronger. That is why the government of Prime Minister Andrew Holness established the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority, NARA. Its mandate is to drive reconstruction at speed and scale, to coordinate major infrastructure projects, crowd in investment, and critically, to embed resilience in the Jamaica we are rebuilding. We're not simply replacing what Melissa has destroyed. We are building the Jamaica that must withstand the storms of tomorrow. Mr. President, Jamaica brings this message to the international community from a position not only of vulnerability, but one of responsibility. Over the past decade, we have undertaken difficult reforms and made difficult decisions. Our debt, which once stood at more than 140% of GDP, was brought down to 62% before Melissa, with unemployment then at a historic low of 3.4%. We built macroeconomic stability, strengthened investor confidence, and created the fiscal space that ultimately helped us respond to the greatest natural disaster in our modern history. We are proud and heartened that, notwithstanding Melissa, Jamaica's credit ratings have either been stabilized or upgraded, and unemployment still stands at a relative low of 3.7%. Those gains did not happen by accident. They required discipline, partnership, sacrifice, consistency, and long-term planning. Our experience has taught us that the strongest response to a crisis begins long before the crisis arrives, in the choices we make, the institutions we build, and the buffers we create. Jamaica will continue to take responsibility for the things within our control, but domestic responsibility must be matched by international solidarity and cooperation. Developing countries cannot reasonably be expected to simultaneously finance climate adaptation, modernize infrastructure, strengthen social protection, manage debt, absorb external shocks, and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals without an international financial system responsive to their realities. Mr. President, that opportunity increasingly depends on technology. Jamaica sees digital transformation and responsible artificial intelligence as powerful tools. The Pact for the Future, the Global Digital Compact, and the Abbas provide important foundations. Our task now as a global community is to translate commitments into action. Mr. President, development also requires peace and security. For Jamaica and our wider Caribbean region, transnational organized crime remains a serious threat. Jamaica reiterates that call today. Illicit firearms do not manufacture themselves in our communities, they cross borders. Criminal money crosses borders. Criminal networks exploit technology and operate across borders. Our response must therefore also cross borders. We call for stronger cooperation in firearms tracing and interdiction, intelligence and information sharing, financial investigations, and law enforcement capacity building. We also urge major arms and forcing in exporting states to strengthen export controls and post the delivery verification. At home, Jamaica has invested heavily in our security forces, strengthened the legislation, enhanced intelligence gathering, oversight, and transformed policing. The results are remarkable by any standard. In 2025, Jamaica recorded its lowest number of homicides in more than three decades. And in 2026, with even further reductions, the Global Peace Index ranked Jamaica the most peaceful country in the Caribbean. We recognize that there remains work to be done, but the direction is clear. And our objective is not merely fewer crimes. It is a durable ecosystem of peace in which every Jamaican can feel safe, raise a family, do business, and fulfill his or her potential, and retire in paradise. Mr. President, nowhere in our region is the challenge of criminal gangs more devastating than in our CARICOM sister nation of Haiti. Jamaica stands firmly with the Haitian people. We urge sustained international support for the Gang Suppression Force, the Haitian National Police, and its armed forces. This support must include the financial, logistical, and operational resources necessary to restore security. We further call for the Security Council to renew the mandate of the GSF at this imperfect but particularly critical juncture. We are at a crossroads. Our own journey has taught us that vulnerability need not mean helplessness, that discipline creates resilience, that partnership multiplies possibility, and that even in moments of profound crisis, nations can choose to build forward. So let us restore trust through what we do. Let us manage transformation with purpose. Let us bring the same seriousness to preventing crises that we do to responding to them. And let us never lose sight of the simple idea on which this institution was founded, that nations working together can achieve what none of us can achieve alone. That is the United Nations Jamaica believes in. and that is the United Nations we will continue to work towards reforming and renewing. I thank you.

Zambia's democratic journey and the 2026 elections. May peace be upon all of us. 81 years ago, from the ashes of the Second World War, Indonesia and the United Nations were born. For eight decades, We have worked to turn that promise into progress. Nations freed themselves from colonialism. Globalization connected our economy. Technology transformed our societies. And development improves the lives of billions. But progress has never been linear. We have lived through financial crisis, a global pandemic, climate disasters, geopolitical rivalries and conflicts around the world. With every transformation and every crisis, one lesson remains clear. For peace and prosperity to endure, multilateralism must be resilient. It must be able to adapt, to respond, and most importantly, to deliver. Because multilateralism that cannot deliver will lose people's trust. And without trust, multilateralism will never endure. Building resilient multilateralism begins with resilient nations. It starts at home. And Indonesia has long understood this for decades. In the 1960s, Indonesia developed the concept of national resilience to safeguard our identity, to protect our sovereignty and unity, and to sustain our development in the face of challenges and obstacles. At the heart of our resilience are our people. A nation is resilient when families can provide for their households, when farmers can produce when workers can find decent jobs, and when children can learn, grow, and dream about their future. For Indonesia, this means building greater self-sufficiency in food and strengthening our energy security. Most importantly, this also means investing in the future of our people, ensuring our children receive quality education and ensuring our people have access to essential healthcare. At the same time, we are building an economy that can withstand shocks and create opportunities, more jobs, stronger industries, and greater productive capacity. Central to our resilience is our ability to manage differences and preserve our unity.

As a nation of more than 280 million people, Indonesia has learned that diversity is not something to overcome. It is something to manage, respect, and turn into strength. Through democratic participation, dialogue, and respect for differences, we preserve our unity. From Aceh to Papua, From Yangas to Rote, Indonesia is one people. Indonesia is one nation. We also continue to strengthen the promotion and protection of human rights through our national mechanisms and our commitment to international human rights obligations. This goes hand in hand with building our national resilience, because human rights are not only the absence of violence, They are also about ensuring that people have food, education, and healthcare. To our neighbors, friends, and partners, let there be no doubt, Indonesia stands strong today, grounded firmly in democracy, human rights, and the rule of law. And when nations are resilient at home, they have greater capacity to contribute beyond their borders. A food secure Indonesia can contribute more to regional and global food security. A more energy resilient Indonesia can contribute more to the global energy transition. A stronger economy opens greater opportunities for cooperation and shared prosperity. This is how national resilience becomes collective resilience. And this is how resilience helps us advance the SDGs. Mr. President, a resilient nation contributes to a resilient region. Our national resilience will support and complement a region that is stable, peaceful, and predictable. Southeast Asia is home to one of the world's largest productive age populations. It is now the world's fifth largest economy, supported by a large and fast growing digital economy. At the center of this dynamic region is ASEAN. ASEAN brings together nations with different histories, political systems, level of development, and national interest. We do not always agree, but we have made a conscious choice to stay together. And we choose to keep talking, even when agreement is difficult. For almost six decades, ASEAN has managed differences, maintained communication, and continued seeking common ground. This is the strength that comes from ASEAN unity and centrality. It enables us to engage all partners and preserve space for dialogue and cooperation. even as a strategic competition intensifies around us. At the same time, building a resilient region requires the ability to adapt. This is why ASEAN must continue to evolve so that it remains fit for purpose and beneficial for its people and the wider region. Excellencies, resilience at home and at the regional level must be matched by a multilateral system capable of supporting and sustaining it. This is where the United Nations remain indispensable. The United Nations give nations the space to resolve differences without resorting to conflict. It provides common rules when interests compete. And it allows us to combine our capacities when no country can act effectively alone. This is why Indonesia continues to believe in the United Nations. But believing in the United Nations also means believing that it must evolve with the world it serves. Let us be clear that the answer to imperfect multilateralism is not less multilateralism. It is a stronger and better multilateralism. A multilateral system fit for the 21st century must be more representative, more agile and better able to deliver. Institutional transformation will not happen overnight, but the urgency of today's challenges requires us to act now. We must start by strengthening our collective capacity to withstand crisis, responding effectively to global crisis and humanitarian situations, and sustaining peace development and cooperation. At the same time, international financial architecture must also evolve to respond better to the needs of developing countries and to give them greater space to pursue their own development priorities and build their resilience. But stronger institutions alone will not save multilateralism. Institutions are only as strong as the principles we are willing to uphold. International law must be upheld consistently. Sovereignty must be respected. And colonialism must be brought to an end. This is where Palestine remains one of the clearest tests of these principles and the test of our conscience. The clear violation of international law in Gaza and the West Bank are reminiscent of our world pre-1945, a world pre the UN Charter, pre the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and pre the four 1949 Geneva Conventions. A world where a certain race was almost annihilated. Indonesia knows what it means to struggle against colonialism. to struggle in a world where international law was weak and might was right. Our nation's journey to independence has shaped our consistent support for the Palestinian people and their right to determine their own future. Indonesia will continue to stand with the Palestinian people until their right to self-determination is fulfilled and until an independent and sovereign state of Palestine is realized based on the two-state solution in accordance with international law and internationally agreed parameters. Palestine is not only a question for one region. It is a test of whether multilateral system can uphold the very principles it was created to defend and whether it can deliver when it matters most. Mr. President, an effective multilateral system also requires effective leadership. Indonesia's leadership philosophy passed down through generations teaches us that leaders must possess the capability to lead by example from the front, build confidence while standing among the people, and empower from behind. Leadership is not simply about commanding. It is about exercising wisdom and giving others the strength to move forward. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has led this organization through an exceptionally challenging period. wars and geopolitical tensions, a global pandemic, humanitarian emergencies, and rapid technological transformation. Indonesia expresses its appreciation for his leadership and service over the past decade. Throughout these challenges, the UN continues to provide an important platform for dialogue and collective problem solving. The next Secretary-General will carry an equally important responsibility to uphold the Charter, strengthen the Organization, and to translate multilateralism into concrete results for people. Effective leadership must also be accompanied with the full commitment of Member States to make multilateralism work. Indonesia is prepared to carry its share, as our constitution mandates us to contribute to a world based on freedom, lasting peace, and social justice. Through diplomacy and mediation, Indonesia has contributed to resolving conflicts in the region and beyond. We have been among the top-tier contributors to UN peacekeeping missions. deploying personnel to missions around the world since 1957. For nearly two decades, Indonesian peacekeepers have served under the UN flag in Lebanon. UNIFIL may be entering its final chapter, but Indonesia's commitment does not end with the mission. The experience sacrifice, and dedication of our peacekeepers will continue to shape Indonesia's contribution to international peace and security. We will carry our diplomacy forward through humanitarian assistance, through peace building, and through engagement across regions and institutions. Mr. President, it is in this spirit that Indonesia present its candidature for a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for the 2029-2030 term. Our commitment is clear. Fostering unity, advancing peace. Fostering unity means rebuilding trust in the multilateral system and keeping channels of dialogue open. Advancing peace requires us to uphold international law and make effective use of the tools available to us. Indonesia will work to keep dialogue open, build common ground, and turn shared responsibility into practical cooperation. We will uphold the UN Charter consistently to maintain international peace and security. We will bring the same principle that guides our foreign policy to engage with all and keep the space for cooperation open. As President Prabowo Subianto mentioned in his very lecture last year, 1,000 friends are too few and an enemy is too many. The same approach guides Indonesia's engagement with all partners. Through ASEAN, G20, D8, BRICS, MICTA, and the UN, Indonesia will extend the friendship to deliver practical cooperation. Mr. President, 81 years ago, Indonesia fought against colonialism so we could chart our own future. Today, we reaffirm our promise for a future peace we all share. Also, one year ago, President Prabowo Subianto called upon us to draw closer, not drift apart. Today, I carry that call forward, and as we draw closer, Let us also make each other stronger. Strong enough for our nations to withstand crisis, strong enough for our regions to preserve cooperation, strong enough for our institutions to deliver for people. Because resilience is not simply about surviving the storms. It is about having the strength to keep moving forward together. And only through our collective resilience Can the United Nations be strong enough to fulfill the promise we made 81 years ago, a future of peace for generations to come?

I thank you.
